tldr: By adding a lightweight control layer called OIL on top of a frozen whole-body controller, which takes desired object motion and contact flags as input, a single policy achieves diverse whole-body behaviors like pushing, pulling, and pick-and-place without task-specific retraining.
hero_caption: Overview of OIL. By adding an object interaction layer on top of an existing whole-body controller, diverse loco-manipulation behaviors—such as approaching, lifting, transporting, placing, and sliding boxes—can be executed by a single controller without task-specific retraining.
overview:
Loco-manipulation, such as carrying or pushing objects with a humanoid robot, is one of the ultimate goals of whole-body control (WBC). Recently, reinforcement learning-based WBC tracking kinematic targets for end-effectors and joints has advanced significantly, enabling robust locomotion without falling. However, conventional WBC only accepts robot-centric commands specifying how the robot should move its own body, without directly handling the intention of how to contact or move an object. As a result, separate controllers had to be retrained for every object-handling task.

To solve this, the authors propose a hierarchical approach by placing an Object Interaction Layer (OIL) on top of an existing, frozen WBC. OIL receives kinematic commands including desired object position, left and right end-effector target positions, and contact conditions (whether to establish contact), and converts them into the arm joint commands required by the WBC. Because lower-body balance and locomotion are completely left to the proven WBC, object-centric motions can be flexibly generated without compromising foot stability.

In simulation experiments on the bipedal robot Digit, a single policy was trained on five primitive behaviors: uni-manual sliding, bi-manual sliding, pick-and-place, loco-transport, and pushing a large box. As a result, it significantly outperformed an object-agnostic baseline and achieved success rates comparable to or better than task-specific policies trained individually. Furthermore, the authors demonstrated zero-shot adaptation to objects with sizes and masses outside the training range, long-horizon composite sequences chaining multiple behaviors, and sim-to-real transfer on the physical Digit humanoid robot.
contributions: Formulated an "object intent API" that passes desired object motion and contact conditions as first-class inputs to a whole-body controller (WBC).
Proposed the OIL architecture that unifies diverse non-prehensile interactions while preserving locomotion and balance capabilities by only generating arm commands for a frozen WBC.
Demonstrated in simulation that a single policy matches or outperforms task-specific policies trained individually and exhibits high generalization to novel object physical properties.
Achieved zero-shot execution of sequentially composed tasks unseen during training (lift -> transport -> place -> push) and sim-to-real transfer to the physical humanoid robot Digit.

sections.heading: Why humanoids need object-aware whole-body control
sections.summary: While recent whole-body control for humanoids excels at tracking the robot's own trajectories, it struggles to handle object contact and intent directly. This work proposes an extension layer called OIL that accepts desired object motion and contact flags, enabling diverse loco-manipulation with a single policy.
sections.details:
For humanoids to be useful in everyday and industrial environments, they must seamlessly combine behaviors like reaching for shelf items while walking, pushing boxes, and carrying objects with both arms. These behaviors require skillful coordination across the entire body under dynamically changing contact conditions.

Recent reinforcement learning-based whole-body controllers (WBC) have made impressive strides, enabling smooth tracking of end-effector or joint trajectories without falling. However, standard WBC command interfaces remain strictly limited to the robot's own kinematics. Actions such as pushing, pulling, and lifting require entirely different force applications and balance strategies, even when the robot appears to be in a similar posture. Without explicit input regarding how the object should be moved, the controller must implicitly infer it from the robot's motion, limiting robustness and generality.

Although methods that generate dedicated trajectories and retrain controllers for each task have been proposed, requiring retraining for every motion prevents a truly general interface. In response, this paper proposes placing an Object Interaction Layer (OIL) over an existing, frozen WBC to receive desired object motion and contact flags. This enables an upstream planner or operator to generate diverse loco-manipulation behaviors with a single policy simply by supplying geometric target trajectories for the object and end-effectors, without calculating forces or balance at all.

captions.F1: Overview of diverse behaviors achieved by OIL. A single controller handles approaching boxes, picking them up from various heights and locations, carrying them while walking, placing them on platforms, and pushing them with one or both hands.

sections.heading: The evolution of whole-body control and moving beyond task-specific controllers
sections.summary: Conventional whole-body control remains confined to robot-centric commands, and most object manipulation studies require individual policies or trajectory optimization per task. OIL overcomes this limitation by integrating object motion and contact as reusable runtime commands.
sections.details:
Related work can be broadly categorized into four lines of research:

- Whole-body Humanoid Control: Reinforcement learning has enabled rough-terrain locomotion and disturbance rejection, while motion-capture imitation has yielded rich whole-body motions. However, these are robot-centric designs tracking joysticks or end-effector positions, without direct input of object interaction intent.
- Trajectory-Guided Loco-Manipulation: Approaches that pre-compute coordinated robot-object trajectories and contact forces via optimization, teleoperation, or video imitation, and train policies to track them. While highly effective, they require data collection and retraining for each new trajectory or task.
- Task-Specific Object Interaction: End-to-end reinforcement learning methods for tasks like wall climbing or box carrying, which incur high costs for designing task-specific reward weightings and state machines.
- Whole-Body Manipulation for Simulated Characters: Studies that achieve diverse manipulations with a single policy for high-DOF computer animation characters, but without targeting deployment to physical humanoid hardware or considering physical hardware constraints.

OIL has a very clear positioning. Instead of rebuilding policies for every task, it introduces an object- and contact-aware extension to the WBC input interface itself, enabling a single trained policy to adapt instantly to arbitrary trajectories.

sections.heading: Formulating directives for object goals and contact conditions
sections.summary: The authors define interaction directives that specify kinematic target trajectories and contact conditions over a finite horizon rather than forces or torques. The controller takes these coarse geometric commands and automatically resolves unspecified contact forces and lower-body balance.
sections.details:
This work targets non-prehensile bimanual manipulation—such as pushing, pulling, or squeezing objects between both hands or palms—without using precision grippers. Upstream systems (planners or teleoperators) can specify behaviors simply by supplying high-level geometric motion directives without reasoning about force control or complex inverse kinematics.

A directive $d_t$ is split into an interaction directive $d^i_t$ for the object and hands, and a base directive $d^b_t$ for the lower body.
- Interaction Directive: Composed of $d^i_t = (\hat{o}_t, \hat{p}^R_t, \hat{p}^L_t, \hat{c}^R_t, \hat{c}^L_t)$, where $\hat{o}_t \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the target object position in the robot frame, $\hat{p}^R_t, \hat{p}^L_t \in \mathbb{R}^3$ are target positions for the right and left end-effectors, and $\hat{c}^R_t, \hat{c}^L_t \in \{0, 1\}$ are binary flags indicating whether contact should be established between the object and hands.
- Base Directive: Represented as $d^b_t = (\hat{v}_t, \hat{\omega}_t, \hat{b}_t)$, specifying the base target planar velocity, yaw velocity, and base orientation.

The controller $\pi^{\mathrm{OI}}$ receives the robot proprioception $r_t$, object state $o_t$, and directive $d_t$ at every step, and outputs PD control target angles for all actuators. Crucially, because the physical hardware lacks end-effector contact sensors, contact states are not included in the observations. The controller must handle contact conditions implicitly through object motion and proprioceptive feedback.

sections.heading: Leveraging a stable foundation: OIL architecture design
sections.summary: By completely freezing a proven whole-body controller (MHC), OIL places a 2-layer LSTM on top to output arm joint targets. A masking technique also allows a single model to unify contact-rich manipulation with free-space end-effector position tracking.
sections.details:
### Overall Architecture
OIL uses a remarkably clever structure. It completely freezes the parameters of the base WBC, which already provides robust locomotion stability and disturbance rejection, and mounts OIL ($\pi^{\mathrm{OIL}}$) on top as a thin additional layer.

### Role of the Whole-Body Controller (WBC)
For the base WBC, the authors adopt the Masked Humanoid Controller (MHC) from prior work. MHC features a "loco-manipulation mode" that handles lower-body walking and balance control while simultaneously tracking upper-body joint targets. Denoting MHC as $\pi^{\mathrm{WBC}}(r_t, d^b_t, u_t)$, it takes base directives $d^b_t$ and arm joint targets $u_t \in \mathbb{R}^8$ (4 DOFs per arm $\times 2$) and outputs joint PD targets $a_t$ for all 20 DOFs.

### Operation of OIL and Masking
The core of OIL is very lightweight, consisting of a 2-layer LSTM with 64 hidden units and a linear decoder. Taking robot state $r_t$, object state $o_t$, and interaction directives $d^i_t$ as input, OIL generates arm joint commands $u_t = \pi^{\mathrm{OIL}}(r_t, o_t, d^i_t)$ to feed into MHC.
A key technique here is unifying free-space hand tracking via input masking. By masking object-related inputs (object position and contact flags) with a certain probability during training and providing only hand targets, OIL learns to handle both contact-rich object manipulation and free-space end-effector tracking within the exact same policy. This enables seamless control through a unified interface without requiring an explicit mode switcher.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of the OIL control system. Among commands provided by the upstream behavior generator, the base directive $d^b_t$ is passed directly to the WBC, while object and hand targets $d^i_t$ are converted by OIL into arm joint targets $u_t$ and passed to the WBC.

sections.heading: Building a hardware-ready policy through curriculum training and domain randomization
sections.summary: A two-stage curriculum gradually increases difficulty from free-space hand tracking to object manipulation. By combining five primitive behaviors with thorough domain randomization that includes simulated perception latency, the policy acquires robustness for sim-to-real deployment.
sections.details:
### Episode Generation and Two-Stage Curriculum
Training is performed in the MuJoCo simulator using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Because the WBC weights are fixed, only the lightweight OIL network is trained.
Training progresses through a two-stage curriculum:
- Stage 1 (Hand Tracking): Object inputs are masked, and the policy practices having the arms track randomly generated hand target positions in free space.
- Stage 2 (Object Interaction): Full object manipulation directives are introduced. Each episode samples object manipulation with an 80% probability and free-space tracking without an object with a 20% probability.

### Five Primitive Behaviors and Skill Chaining
Stage 2 designs five behaviors covering essential loco-manipulation elements:
- Uni-manual Slide: Pushing a box forward with one hand.
- Bi-manual Slide: Squeezing a box with both hands while sliding it across a table.
- Pick-and-place: Squeezing a box with both hands, lifting it, and setting it down elsewhere.
- Loco-transport: Walking forward, backward, or turning while carrying a lifted box.
- Large-box Push: Pushing a box too large to carry with both hands while walking forward.
These do not have task labels or explicit phase-switching flags; they are provided to the policy as time-varying directive sequences.

### Reward Design and Domain Randomization
The reward consists of five components: hand tracking, object pose tracking, contact matching, regularization, and collision penalties. For object tracking, position errors of two fixed points (constellation points)—the center of mass and another point—are evaluated to penalize orientation errors as well. In lifting tasks, contact rewards also evaluate whether sufficient upward normal force is generated to support the object.
To prepare for real-robot transfer, object mass (0.1 to 3.0 kg), friction coefficients (0.5 to 1.5), and dimensions are heavily randomized. Crucially, perception latency is also simulated: to model processing delays from external cameras on real hardware, object updates are randomly varied between 7 and 15 Hz, holding previous values between updates.

sections.heading: Single policy rivals specialized controllers: Remarkable generalization and real-robot validation
sections.summary: Achieving an average success rate of 90.4% across five tasks, OIL matched or exceeded specialized policies trained on each task individually. It proved robust to out-of-distribution physical properties, succeeded at zero-shot task composition, and transferred successfully to the physical Digit robot.
sections.details:
### Baseline Comparisons (Results from Table 1)
The authors evaluated 5,000 trials per task in simulation, comparing against $\text{MHC}_{\text{NoObj}}$ (which lacks object information) and task-specific policies trained individually.
OIL recorded an average success rate of 90.4% across all tasks, vastly outperforming the 51.0% achieved by $\text{MHC}_{\text{NoObj}}$. The performance gap was especially pronounced in locomotion-coupled tasks: loco-transport rose from 15.8% to 84.1%, and large-box pushing climbed from 18.3% to 84.6%. These figures prove that looking only at the robot's body is insufficient for carrying or pushing; object intent is essential. Remarkably, the unified OIL policy even outperformed task-specific policies in both average success rate (90.4% vs. 88.4%) and average object tracking error (2.28 cm vs. 2.76 cm).

### Generalization to Unseen Physical Properties
Robustness was evaluated on object sizes and masses outside the training distribution. When box width exceeded the training maximum, the task-specific policy dropped to roughly 85% success, whereas OIL maintained over 95%. When mass was increased beyond the 3.0 kg training limit up to 7.0 kg, the task-specific policy dropped below 50% at 6.5 kg, but OIL remained above 80%. Learning diverse motions concurrently appears to foster flexible recovery from trajectory deviations.

### Zero-Shot Sequential Task Composition
A four-stage composite sequence—lift $\rightarrow$ loco-transport $\rightarrow$ place on table $\rightarrow$ bi-manual slide—was evaluated over 10,000 episodes without switching policies or additional training. Success rate drops between stages were minimal, reaching a final full-sequence success rate of 78.9%.

### Sim-to-Real Transfer on Digit and Limitations
OIL was deployed zero-shot to a physical Digit V3 using an overhead external camera (RealSense D455) and ArUco markers to track the robot and object. Without any policy fine-tuning, the robot successfully performed uni-manual and bi-manual sliding, pick-and-place, and loco-transport.
The paper also analyzes failure modes. When one-handed pushing contact drifted off-center, causing the box to rotate, or when low friction caused a box to slip from the hands, the system currently lacked a mechanism to autonomously recover once contact was broken.

captions.F3: Robustness comparison on out-of-distribution (OOD) physical properties. In both widening box width (left) and increasing mass (right, with red dashed line marking the training maximum), the single OIL policy (orange) exhibits significantly higher resilience than the task-specific policy (blue).
captions.F4: Success rates across phases during continuous execution of four chained tasks. Without switching policies, the controller smoothly transitions from lifting to walking, placing, and sliding, achieving a high end-to-end completion rate of 78.9%.

sections.heading: Appendix: Directive generation and parameter details supporting training
sections.summary: The appendix details hand and walking velocity sampling ranges, state transition phases for each behavior, domain randomization parameters, and reward weightings used during training.
sections.details:
The appendix provides detailed experimental parameters to ensure reproducibility.

- Directive Sampling: Hand positions are sampled uniformly in the robot base frame within a collision-free workspace. Loco-transport velocity directives cover a wide range: forward velocity $v_x \in [-0.5, 0.8]$ m/s, lateral velocity $v_y \in [-0.3, 0.3]$ m/s, and yaw rate $\omega \in [-0.4, 0.4]$ rad/s.
- Phase Transitions and Skill Chaining: Each task is structured as a chain of geometric generation phases such as align, approach, contact, and lift, transitioning automatically based on predetermined durations $\tau_i$. No phase labels are provided to the policy.
- Environment and Object Setup: Initial table height ranges from 0.01 to 1.15 m to match the robot's crouching range, accommodating everything from large floor boxes to small desktop items.
- Reward Weighting: In addition to hand and object tracking error terms, smoothness regularizations penalizing excessive torque and abrupt action changes, along with body-environment collision penalties, are finely tuned to ensure safe behavior on hardware.

takeaways: Contact-rich loco-manipulation can be achieved without modifying or retraining a whole-body controller (WBC), simply by adding a thin object interaction layer on top.
Explicitly providing desired object motion and contact flags as inputs—rather than just robot posture—is crucial for dramatically boosting success in carrying and pushing tasks.
Training a single policy on diverse behavior sequences naturally builds superior adaptability to unseen masses and sizes compared to task-specific policies.

When low-level locomotion and balance control are already robust, applying domain randomization for perception latency and physical properties to the higher-level layer enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
limitations: Because the policy lacks contact or force sensor observations, it cannot autonomously recover or retry when an object slips from the hands or rotates due to off-center contact.
End-effector manipulation is restricted to non-prehensile actions like squeezing and pushing, without yet supporting dexterous grasping with multi-fingered hands.
Full 3D rotational control (full SE(3) pose) and autonomous obstacle-avoiding trajectory generation are not handled by the control layer alone and rely on upstream planners.
